report.headline: Verdict: 'Dead patent with a future' (87/100, high confidence). The core idea sits in a busy, active field, but the space around it appears crowded with newer patents.
report.what_it_is: This patent covers a water-cleaning device that pulls salts and other ions out of water by charging porous electrodes. Its key addition is an extra 'charge barrier' layer next to each electrode, which keeps stray ions on one side so the device cleans water more efficiently.

why_it_died.text: It did not die early. It ran its full term and ended on 2021-04-18. The owner, a large company, paid every maintenance fee until the end, which suggests they valued it. That is why the 'died for money, not merit' score is only middling (7.5/15): it simply aged out, rather than being dropped as a bargain someone overlooked.

case_for.point: The field still appears active. Many later filings cite it, including recent ones from 2019 onward and several from unrelated owners after it expired.
Known companies have been building on this area recently, including Robert Bosch and several startups. That suggests ongoing technical and commercial interest.

Capacitive deionization products already exist. Navien sells one as a salt-free softener alternative, and suppliers list uses like softening, heavy metal removal and nitrate removal. So there may be buyers to sell to.
Examiners cited it against 105 later applications. Its first claim was fairly broad, which suggests it describes a foundational idea in the field.

case_against.point: The original owner may still be a competitor. Voltea filed later related patents that may still be in force, including a membrane-capacitive deionization system.
The space appears crowded. About 70 later patents by other owners were cited against this one and may still be in force. Newer improvements may be covered even though this patent ended.
Market size is unproven. The signals show interest and one product on the market, not revenue or demand.
The patent explains the idea, not how to make it well at scale. Expect to build the manufacturing know-how yourself.

blockers.point: Later patents by the original owner that cite this one may still be in force. Worth checking before designing.
About 70 later patents by other owners may still be in force in this area. A modern product could touch some of them.
Drinking water products usually need NSF/ANSI 61 certification. Discharge systems need EPA or state permits. That adds cost and time.
Manufacturing know-how is not in the patent. Electrode and barrier materials will need to be developed in-house.

assumption_to_test.assumption: A specific buyer group (for example homeowners or small commercial sites wanting salt-free softening) will pay for a new capacitive deionization product over established options like Navien's WEC Series or salt softeners.
assumption_to_test.why_riskiest: The technology already has commercial players, so the business depends on finding buyers who are unhappy with what exists and will switch. The evidence shows interest, not demand or pricing.
assumption_to_test.how_to_test: Within two weeks: interview 15 water treatment dealers or installers about why customers do or don't pick salt-free softeners like Navien's, and what price and performance would make them switch. In parallel, run a $200 landing page offering a salt-free softener and measure sign-ups or quote requests.

attorney_questions: Do Voltea's later patents citing this one, such as EP3995458A1, have US counterparts still in force that could matter for a charge-barrier capacitor design?
Which of the roughly 70 later patents cited against this one appear most relevant to a modern charge-barrier deionization product, and are they still in force?
What would a focused freedom-to-operate search cost for a specific product design in this area, and what should we prepare first?
report.disclaimer: Research and triage only, not legal advice. This report is not a patentability, validity or freedom-to-operate opinion. Patent status shown here comes from public records that can lag or be wrong. An expired patent is not the same as free to use: follow-on patents, regulatory exclusivity, trade secrets and standards can still block a product. Confirm with a registered patent attorney before acting.

signals.signal: The capacitive deionization field this patent sits in still draws new technical filings, including after the patent's term ended.
The patent is a foundational reference in the field. Examiners have cited it heavily and its total forward citations are high, which points to broad technical relevance rather than proven revenue.
Capacitive deionization products and applications are being marketed today, especially water softening as an alternative to salt-based softeners.
The original owner paid every maintenance fee and claimed large-entity status, which suggests it valued the patent through its full term.

read.who_is_active: Since 2019, filings building on this patent have come from Robert Bosch GmbH, Siontech, VWS (UK), Summit Nanotech, Pani Clean and the University of Kentucky Research Foundation. Navien markets a capacitive deionization softener, and Voltea is associated with the technology, though its current product line was not checked.
read.market_read: Capacitive deionization appears to be an active niche, with recent filings from industrial and startup players and at least one commercial softening product on the market. These signals show sustained technical and commercial interest, but they do not establish market size or revenue, so a founder should validate demand and the specific competitive and patent landscape directly before committing.

web.finding: Navien sells the WEC Series, a capacitive deionization water filtration system with an electric adsorption/regeneration process, marketed as an alternative to salt-based softeners.
Voltea has a Wikipedia page that cites a Wageningen University source on capacitive deionization for energy-efficient drinking water production; its current product line was not checked.
Water-treatment supplier Lenntech lists capacitive deionization applications including water softening, heavy metal removal, and phosphate/nitrate removal.
